paras: The attempted lynching of Jones at Pocahontas, Mississippi, was a mob gathering reported on August 8, 1900, to lynch a Black man named Jones who had been arrested the day before on a charge of assaulting a white woman. Sheriff Harding and a posse of deputies set out from Jackson to stop it, and the coverage does not report what followed.

According to the dispatch, Jones, described as "a negro," was arrested on August 7, "charged with assaulting a white woman." The papers give no first name for him and no name or other detail for the woman.

On August 8 a message reached Jackson that a mob was gathering at Pocahontas, sixteen miles away, to lynch Jones. In response, Sheriff Harding started for the town that day with a posse of deputies. The dispatch was sent before the posse arrived, and the Wichita version closed with the line "Trouble is feared."
No later report on whether the sheriff reached Pocahontas in time, whether Jones was harmed or removed, or whether he was tried was found in the coverage.

The episode survives only as a brief wire item from Jackson that ran in two Kansas papers. The Topeka State Journal printed it on August 8 under the headline "A Mob Gathering," while the Wichita Daily Eagle ran it the next day as "Long Way to Save a Negro," adding the closing warning of trouble. Neither paper added comment, and both repeated the charge against Jones as the dispatch gave it.
No Mississippi paper and no Black newspaper in the coverage carried the story.
